Types of Swimming Pools
Two Main Categories for Residential Properties
Above-Ground Pool
Inground Pool

Above-Ground Pools

  • Freestanding structure, 48-54" wall height
  • Installed on prepared ground surface
  • Cost: $1,500-$5,000 (kit, installed)
  • May or may not require a permit
  • Can be disassembled and relocated

Inground Pools

  • Permanent structure built into the ground
  • Concrete (gunite), Vinyl Liner, or Fiberglass
  • Cost: $35,000-$100,000+
  • Always requires a building permit in VA
  • Permanent improvement to real property
Note: In Virginia, any pool holding water to a depth of more than 2 feet may be subject to fencing ordinances under Code of Virginia 15.2-921, regardless of whether it is above-ground or inground.
Safe House Property Inspections3 of 26
Speaker Notes Above-ground pools range from inexpensive temporary setups to substantial semi-permanent installations with decking and filtration. In Virginia, a pool that holds water to a depth of more than 2 feet may be subject to fencing ordinances under Code of Virginia 15.2-921, regardless of whether it is above-ground or inground. Inground pools are permanent structures that add to the property's assessed value and require building permits. The three inground construction types differ significantly in cost, maintenance, and longevity. Concrete pools last the longest but require the most maintenance (acid washing, resurfacing every 10-15 years). Vinyl liner pools need liner replacement every 7-15 years. Fiberglass pools are low-maintenance but have size limitations due to transportation constraints.
Above-Ground Pools in Real Estate Transactions
Personal Property or Real Property?
  • Classification: May be considered personal property or real property depending on permanence of installation
  • Conveyance: Typically excluded from the sale unless specifically included in the contract
  • Documentation: If included, ensure seller provides any permits, warranty, and installation documentation
  • Code Check: Verify whether the pool meets local code (setback, fencing, electrical)
  • Appraisal: If pool has permanent equipment (filtration, decking), it may be included in the appraisal
Key Point: Always clarify in the purchase contract whether an above-ground pool is included or excluded. If it has permanent decking and wiring, it may be considered a fixture that conveys automatically.
Safe House Property Inspections4 of 26
Speaker Notes Above-ground pools occupy a gray area between personal property and real estate. If the pool is simply sitting on the ground and can be removed, it is likely personal property and would not convey with the real estate unless the contract specifically includes it. If the pool has permanent decking, electrical wiring, or is embedded into the ground, it may be considered a fixture and part of the real estate. Always clarify in the purchase contract whether the pool is included or excluded. For VA loans, above-ground pools may be included in the appraisal if they have permanent equipment and if that is customary in the area.
Inground Pools in Real Estate Transactions
Permanent Improvements with Disclosure Obligations
  • Classification: Always considered real property (permanent improvement)
  • Conveyance: Conveys with the real estate unless specifically excluded in the contract
  • Value Impact: Adds to assessed property value and may increase property taxes
  • Construction Types: Concrete (gunite), Vinyl Liner, or Fiberglass — each with different maintenance profiles
  • Disclosure framework: Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act (55.1-703) is a "no representations" statute. Pools are NOT one of the 19 covered topics. The seller makes no warranty about pool condition. This makes buyer due diligence (pool inspection) even MORE critical.
Key Distinction: Virginia's disclosure law is a "no representations" notice, not a condition disclosure. The seller gives the buyer a form saying "I make no representations about the condition of this property" covering 19 specific topics (flood zones, radon, lead pipes, defective drywall, etc.). Pools are NOT on this list. The seller is NOT required to disclose pool defects. This means the buyer's only protection is their own due diligence: hire a pool inspector before ratifying the contract.
One exception: If there is a pending building code or zoning enforcement action related to the pool (e.g., unpermitted installation, fence non-compliance), the seller must affirmatively disclose that under 55.1-703. This is the narrow path where pool issues could trigger a disclosure.
Safe House Property Inspections5 of 26
Speaker Notes Unlike above-ground pools, inground pools are permanent structures that automatically convey with the property. Now, a critical point about Virginia's disclosure law. The Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act, codified at Section 55.1-703, is a "no representations" statute, not a condition disclosure law. The seller gives the buyer a form that says "I make no representations or warranties about the condition of this property." That form covers 19 specific topics, including flood zones, radon, lead pipes, defective drywall, and airport noise. Swimming pools are NOT on that list. This means the seller is NOT required to disclose pool defects, even if they know about them. The buyer's sole protection is their own due diligence. This is why a pool inspection is absolutely critical in Virginia. Without it, the buyer has no way to know the pool's condition. There is one narrow exception: if there is a pending building code or zoning enforcement action related to the pool, the seller must affirmatively disclose that. But routine pool defects, leaks, equipment failures, or code issues that are not under active enforcement do not trigger any disclosure obligation. As an agent, you should understand this framework and strongly recommend pool inspections to your buyer clients.
How a Swimming Pool Works

Safe House Property Inspections6 of 26
Speaker Notes A swimming pool is a recirculating water system with four main subsystems. The suction side pulls water from the pool through the skimmer and main drain. The filtration system pushes that water through the pump and filter to remove debris and contaminants. The pressure side returns clean water to the pool through return jets. Additional components like heaters, chemical feeders, salt chlorine generators, and automation controllers enhance the system but are not required for basic operation. Understanding this flow helps you explain to clients what a pool inspection covers and why certain red flags matter.
Suction Side: Pulling Water from the Pool
Skimmer, Main Drain, and Suction Lines
Skimmer Basket (at waterline)
Main Drain (at pool floor)
  • Skimmer: Surface debris removal; basket catches leaves and insects at the waterline
  • Main Drain: Bottom debris removal; located at the deepest point of the pool
  • Suction Lines: PVC pipes connecting skimmer and main drain to the pump
Safety Critical: Main drains must have compliant anti-entrapment drain covers installed in accordance with the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGB Act). A missing, broken, or non-compliant drain cover is a life-threatening safety hazard. See Slide 22 for details.
Safe House Property Inspections7 of 26
Speaker Notes The suction side is where water leaves the pool. The skimmer sits at the waterline and draws in surface debris through a removable basket. The main drain sits at the bottom of the pool and pulls water from the deep end. Both connect via PVC suction lines to the pump. A critical safety point: main drains must have anti-entrapment drain covers installed in compliance with the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act, a federal law we will discuss in detail on Slide 22. If a main drain cover is missing, broken, or non-compliant, the pool is a serious safety hazard and should be flagged immediately. A pool inspector will check the condition and compliance of drain covers as part of any inspection.
Filtration System: The Pump and Filter
The Heart of the Pool
Pool Pump (on equipment pad)
Pool Filter (on equipment pad)

Pump

  • The "heart" of the pool; circulates water
  • Creates suction (inlet) and pressure (outlet)
  • Types: Single-speed, Dual-speed, Variable-speed
  • Variable-speed required on new installations per DOE rule (2021)

Filter

  • Removes debris and particulates from water
  • Three types: Sand, DE, Cartridge
  • Type determines maintenance and replacement intervals
  • Filter media lifespan differs from tank/housing lifespan
Safe House Property Inspections8 of 26
Speaker Notes The pump is the engine of the pool system. It creates suction on the inlet side and pressure on the outlet side, circulating the entire pool volume through the filter typically once or twice per day. As of July 2021, federal Department of Energy regulations require that all new pool pump motors sold in the U.S. meet certain efficiency standards, which effectively means variable-speed pumps for most new installations. The filter removes particulate matter from the water. The three filter types — sand, DE, and cartridge — each have different maintenance requirements and lifespans, which we will cover on the next slides.
Pressure Side and Optional Equipment
Returning Clean Water + Enhancements
Salt chlorine generator cell installed on equipment pad (labeled: pump, filter, salt cell)

Pressure Side

  • Return Lines: PVC pipes carrying filtered water back to the pool
  • Return Jets: Fittings that return clean water; adjustable direction

Optional Equipment

  • Heater: Gas, electric (heat pump), or solar
  • Chemical Feeder: Dispenses chlorine or sanitizers automatically
  • Salt Chlorine Generator: Converts salt to chlorine via electrolysis
  • Automation Controller: Digital scheduling for pump, heater, lighting
Salt Systems: Salt chlorine generators produce chlorine from dissolved salt. The water feels softer but is NOT "chlorine-free" as some sellers may claim. Salt can also be corrosive to certain pool components.
Safe House Property Inspections9 of 26
Speaker Notes The pressure side returns filtered, chemically treated water to the pool through return jets, which can be aimed to create circulation patterns that help direct debris toward the skimmer. Optional equipment includes heaters (gas, heat pump, or solar), chemical feeders, salt chlorine generators, and automation controllers. Salt systems have become very popular and many buyers ask about them. A salt chlorine generator does not eliminate the need for chlorine; it produces chlorine from dissolved salt through electrolysis. The water feels softer but is not "chlorine-free" as some sellers may claim. If a property has a salt system, note that salt can be corrosive to certain pool components and may require different maintenance than a traditional chlorine pool.
Filter Types and Life Expectancy
Media vs. Tank Lifespan — Don't Conflate Them
Sand Filter
DE Filter
Cartridge Filter
Filter TypeMedia / Element LifeTank / Housing LifeMaintenance
Sand5-7 years (media replacement)15-20+ yearsBackwash every 4-6 weeks
DE (Diatomaceous Earth)2-4 years (grids)7-10 yearsBackwash + recharge with DE powder
Cartridge2-3 years (elements)5-10 yearsRemove and hose clean every 3-6 months
Key Distinction: The filter media (sand, DE grids, cartridge elements) is the consumable part that does the actual filtering. The tank or housing is the structure that holds it. These have very different lifespans. In Virginia's freeze-thaw climate, improper winterization can crack tanks and shorten all equipment life.
Safe House Property Inspections10 of 26
Speaker Notes There is an important distinction between the filter media (the consumable part that does the actual filtering) and the tank or housing (the structure that holds it). Sand filter media typically lasts 5-7 years before it becomes channelized and loses effectiveness, but the fiberglass or plastic tank can last 15-20 years or more. DE filter grids need replacement every 2-4 years, while the tank lasts 7-10 years. Cartridge filter elements last 2-3 years; the housing can last 5-10 years. These ranges assume regular maintenance and proper water chemistry. In Virginia, freeze protection is critical. If a pool is not properly winterized, ice expansion can crack filter tanks, pipes, and pump housings, dramatically shortening equipment life.

8-12 Years for Both Types — Different Failure Modes
Single-Speed Pump (no digital display)
Pump on Equipment Pad
Pump TypeTypical LifeNotes
Single-Speed8-10 yearsOldest technology; one constant speed; being phased out by federal energy standards
Variable-Speed8-12 yearsRequired on new installations per DOE rule (2021); more efficient; electronics may fail before motor

Common Causes of Premature Failure: Power surges, lightning strikes, freeze damage, running dry (no water in pump basket).
Safe House Property Inspections11 of 26
Speaker Notes Pool pumps generally last 8-12 years regardless of type, though the failure modes differ. Single-speed pumps are simpler machines with fewer electronic components, so when they fail it is usually the motor bearings or the seal. Variable-speed pumps have more complex electronics (drive boards, controllers) that can fail independently of the motor. The Department of Energy's new efficiency rule, effective July 2021, effectively requires variable-speed pumps for most new residential pool installations. This means older single-speed pumps are being phased out and replacement pumps will be more expensive. For buyers, a pool with an older single-speed pump may need an $800-$1,500 pump replacement in the near future, and the replacement will be a variable-speed unit.

Virginia Disclosure Law and Pools
The "No Representations" Framework — Why Inspections Matter More
Critical: Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act (55.1-703) is a "no representations" statute. The seller gives the buyer a form stating they make NO warranties about the property's condition. The form covers 19 specific topics. Pools are NOT on the list. The seller is NOT required to disclose pool defects.
  • The 19 covered topics include: adjacent parcels, historic districts, flood zones, wastewater systems, radon, lead pipes, defective drywall, airport noise, and others. Pools, pool equipment, and pool barriers are NOT included
  • What this means for buyers: The buyer's only protection is their own due diligence. A pool inspection is essential because the seller has no obligation to disclose pool condition
  • What this means for sellers: Sellers are not required to disclose pool defects, but they also cannot actively conceal them. Willful misrepresentation is not protected by the Act
  • One narrow exception: If there is a pending building code or zoning enforcement action related to the pool (e.g., unpermitted installation, fence violation), the seller MUST affirmatively disclose that
  • Timing: The disclosure form must be delivered before contract ratification. If delivered late, the buyer can terminate within 3 days of receipt
Agent's Role: Because the law does not require sellers to disclose pool condition, it is YOUR responsibility to recommend a pool inspection to every buyer client. This is not optional advice. It is the buyer's primary protection.
Safe House Property Inspections15 of 26
Speaker Notes This is one of the most important slides in the course. Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act, at Section 55.1-703, is NOT a defect disclosure law. It is a "no representations" statute. The seller gives the buyer a standardized form that says "I make no representations or warranties about the condition of this property." That form covers 19 specific topics: adjacent parcels, historic districts, flood zones, wastewater systems, radon, lead pipes, defective drywall, airport noise, and others. Swimming pools are NOT on that list. This means the seller has NO legal obligation to disclose that the pool leaks, the pump is broken, the heater does not work, or the drain cover is non-compliant. The buyer's only protection is their own due diligence. This is why recommending a pool inspection is not just good practice in Virginia, it is the buyer's primary safeguard. Without it, the buyer has no way to know what they are buying. There is one narrow exception to the disclosure framework: if there is a pending building code or zoning enforcement action related to the pool, the seller must affirmatively disclose that. But routine pool defects do not trigger any disclosure. Also note the timing: the disclosure form must be delivered before contract ratification. If it is delivered late, the buyer's sole remedy is to terminate, generally within 3 days of receipt. The Act does not block other remedies for willful misrepresentation, so if a seller actively conceals a pool defect, that could be a separate fraud claim. But the Act itself does not require pool condition disclosure.
Preparing a Pool Property for Listing
Maximize Appeal, Minimize Liability

Before Listing

  • Professionally clean and service the pool
  • Open it if it is closed
  • Have the pool inspected and repairs completed
  • Stage the pool area: clean decking, tidy landscaping
  • Gather documentation: permits, warranties, service records
  • Professional photography with pool open and clean
  • Ensure fencing and barriers are code-compliant

Seasonal Strategy

  • Fall listing: Have seller close before closing to transfer responsibility cleanly
  • Spring listing: Have seller open before closing so buyer can inspect
  • Winter listing: Disclose that pool is closed and has not been inspected
  • Cost of opening: $200-$400 (often worth it for showing appeal)
Safe House Property Inspections16 of 26
Speaker Notes A clean, well-maintained pool is a selling feature. A dirty or closed pool can be a liability that raises questions about condition and maintenance. If possible, the pool should be open and clean for listing photos and showings. If the pool is closed for winter, buyers may request that it be opened for inspection, or they may write an addendum allowing them to inspect the pool after opening and place funds in escrow pending the result. Agents should counsel sellers that a pool in poor visible condition will likely reduce offers and sale price. The cost of a professional cleaning ($150-$400) is modest compared to the potential reduction in sale price from a neglected-looking pool.
PART 2
Buying with a Pool
Due Diligence, Inspections, and Red Flags
Safe House Property Inspections17 of 26
Speaker Notes Now we shift to the buyer's side. This is where you add the most value as an agent by knowing what to recommend, what to refer out, and what red flags to watch for.
Buying with a Pool: Know Your Scope
Stay in Your Lane — Refer the Rest

Within Your Expertise

  • Provide comparable sales data for pool vs. non-pool homes
  • Explain disclosure obligations and contract contingencies
  • Recommend a professional pool inspection as a contingency
  • Explain the escrow/addendum process for closed pools

Outside Your Expertise

  • What will it cost to maintain? (Refer to pool service company)
  • Is it safe to dive? (Refer to pool inspector)
  • Will it affect my insurance? (Refer to insurance agent)
  • Is the equipment up to code? (Refer to pool inspector or electrician)
Key Principle: The only reliable way for a buyer to understand the condition and cost of a pool is to hire a professional pool inspector and obtain a quote from a pool service company. Your job is to recommend that they do so.
Safe House Property Inspections18 of 26
Speaker Notes One of the most important principles in this course is knowing the boundary between your expertise and other professionals' expertise. As a real estate agent, you can provide market data, explain contract mechanics, and recommend inspections. You should not estimate repair costs, assess electrical safety, or advise on insurance implications. If a buyer asks whether the pool is deep enough to dive safely, that is a question for a pool inspector. If they ask about insurance, refer them to their insurance agent. The only reliable way for a buyer to understand the condition and cost of a pool is to hire a professional pool inspector and obtain a quote from a pool service company.
Pool Inspections and Closed Pools
A Home Inspection Is Not a Pool Inspection
Professional pool inspection
Closed pool (winterized)
  • Hire a certified pool inspector (CPO, CPI, or similar certification) — not just a home inspector
  • Inspection covers: Structure, equipment, electrical bonding, safety barriers, drain cover compliance, water chemistry
  • Cost: Typically $250-$500
If the Pool Is Closed:
  1. Have the seller open the pool for inspection ($200-$400)
  2. Or write an addendum: buyer has right to inspect after opening, with escrow funds held until inspection is complete
  • Choosing a pool inspector: Ask for certifications, verify insurance and licensing, request a sample report
Safe House Property Inspections19 of 26
Speaker Notes A standard home inspection may include a visual check of the pool but is not a substitute for a dedicated pool inspection. A certified pool operator (CPO) or certified pool inspector (CPI) will examine the pool structure, circulation system, electrical bonding and grounding, safety barriers, drain cover compliance, and water chemistry. If the pool is closed for winter, the buyer has two options: ask the seller to open it for inspection, or write an addendum allowing a post-closing inspection with escrow funds held until the pool can be opened and inspected. The escrow approach shifts some risk to the buyer but can be negotiated. Ideally, negotiate the pool to be opened and inspected before closing so both parties know what they are dealing with.
Pool Red Flags: What to Watch For
Recognize and Refer — Do Not Diagnose
Red flag: Green water indicates algae bloom or sanitation failure. This pool needs professional service before any transaction.

Structural

  • Cracks in pool shell (hairline vs. structural)
  • Loose, cracked, or missing tiles
  • Deck cracking, heaving, or settling
  • Vinyl liner tears, wrinkles, or staining

Equipment

  • Rust on equipment pad, pump, or heater
  • Noisy pump (worn bearings, imminent failure)
  • Leaking valves or fittings
  • Non-compliant or missing drain covers

Water Quality

  • Cloudy or green water (filtration failure)
  • Staining (metal content or algae)
  • Strong chlorine smell (chloramines, not clean)

Electrical

  • Missing or inadequate bonding/grounding (NEC Art. 680)
  • Non-GFCI protected circuits
  • Extension cords running pool equipment
Safe House Property Inspections20 of 26
Speaker Notes These red flags fall into four categories: structural, equipment, water quality, and electrical. The most serious are electrical issues, particularly missing or inadequate bonding and grounding, which can create a lethal shock hazard. Non-compliant drain covers are also a critical safety issue under the Virginia Graeme Baker Act. Cloudy or green water suggests the pool has not been maintained, which may indicate deeper problems. A noisy pump often means the bearings are failing and the pump will need replacement soon. Deck cracking or heaving can indicate a plumbing leak beneath the deck, which is a costly repair. As an agent, your job is not to diagnose these issues but to recognize them and recommend a professional pool inspection.

Virginia Pool Laws and Regulations
Fencing, Building Code, Maintenance Code, and Federal Safety

Speaker Notes Now we get into the legal framework. This is the section the DPOR Education Committee will scrutinize most carefully. Every citation must be accurate.
Virginia Pool Fencing Law
Code of Virginia 15.2-921 — Ordinances Requiring Fencing of Swimming Pools
RequirementDetail
Minimum fence height4 feet (48 inches) above ground surface
Ground clearanceWithin 2 inches of the ground at the bottom
Setback from poolAt least 5 feet from pool edge at any point
"Swimming pool" definitionAny outdoor man-made structure holding water to a depth of more than 2 feet
Gate requirementMust be capable of being securely fastened at 4+ feet height
PenaltyFine up to $300 and/or 30 days in jail (Class 4 misdemeanor)
ApplicabilityApplies to pools built both before and after ordinance adoption
Important: This statute authorizes local ordinances. Local jurisdictions may adopt stricter requirements. Fairfax County, Arlington County, and others require 48-inch barriers with self-closing, self-latching gates. Always check the specific locality.
Safe House Property Inspections22 of 26
Speaker Notes Code of Virginia Section 15.2-921 is the enabling statute that allows Virginia localities to pass pool fencing ordinances. It sets the minimum standards: a 4-foot fence, 2-inch ground clearance, 5-foot setback from the pool edge, and self-fastening gates. However, this is a floor, not a ceiling. Local jurisdictions can and do adopt stricter requirements. Fairfax County, Arlington County, and many others require 48-inch barriers with self-closing, self-latching gates, and some restrict horizontal rail placement to prevent climbing. When advising clients, always check the local jurisdiction's specific ordinance. A pool that meets the state minimum but violates a local ordinance is still a code violation and can delay or prevent a sale.
Building Code, Maintenance Code, and Disclosure
Three Additional Legal Frameworks

1. Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code (VUSBC) — New Construction

  • Adopts the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code (ISPSC) and IRC Appendix V
  • Requires 48-inch minimum barrier, 4-inch max sphere openings, self-closing/self-latching gates

2. Virginia Maintenance Code (VMC), Section 303.2 — Existing Pools

  • Requires pool barriers be maintained as required by the code under which they were constructed
  • If a barrier falls into disrepair, the owner is responsible for restoring it

3. Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act (55.1-703)

  • A "no representations" statute, NOT a defect disclosure law
  • Seller gives buyer a form covering 19 specific topics. Pools are NOT on the list
  • Seller has NO obligation to disclose pool condition or defects
  • One exception: Must affirmatively disclose any pending building code or zoning enforcement action the seller actually knows about
  • Practical impact: Because the law does not require pool disclosure, buyer due diligence (pool inspection) is the primary protection
Safe House Property Inspections23 of 26
Speaker Notes There are three additional legal frameworks beyond the fencing statute. First, the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code governs new pool construction and adopts the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code and IRC Appendix V, which specify barrier heights, gate requirements, and construction standards. Second, the Virginia Maintenance Code, specifically Section 303.2, requires that existing pool barriers be maintained to the standard under which they were built. This means that if a pool's fence falls into disrepair, the owner is in violation even if the pool was originally compliant. Third, the Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act at Section 55.1-703. This is a "no representations" statute, not a defect disclosure law. The seller gives the buyer a form covering 19 specific topics, and pools are NOT on that list. The seller has no obligation to disclose pool condition or defects. The one narrow exception is that the seller must affirmatively disclose any pending building code or zoning enforcement action they actually know about. So if the locality has cited the property for an unpermitted pool or a fence violation, that must be disclosed. But a leaking pool, a broken pump, or a non-compliant drain cover does not trigger any disclosure obligation under this Act. This is why pool inspections are so critical in Virginia: they are the buyer's primary, and often only, protection. As an agent, you should understand all three layers and direct clients to the local building department for specific requirements.
Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGB Act)
Federal Anti-Entrapment Safety Law — Public Law 110-140 (2007)
UNSAFE: Flat drain (entrapment risk)
SAFE: VGB-compliant domed cover
  • What it is: Federal law enacted in 2007, administered by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC)
  • Named after: Virginia Graeme Baker, a 7-year-old who died in a suction entrapment incident in 2002
  • Requires: All public pools and spas (including hotel, apartment, and community pools) to have anti-entrapment drain covers
  • Residential pools: Not strictly mandated by federal law, but Virginia building codes may require compliance on new construction or renovation
Safety Hazard: A pool with a missing, broken, or non-compliant drain cover is a life-threatening entrapment hazard. Pool inspectors must verify drain cover compliance. Buyers should be informed of the safety implications. This is a red flag that should be addressed before closing.
Safe House Property Inspections24 of 26
Speaker Notes The Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act is the most important pool safety law in the United States. It was passed in 2007 after a 7-year-old girl, Virginia Graeme Baker, died when the suction from a spa drain trapped her underwater. The law requires anti-entrapment drain covers on all public pools and spas, which includes pools at hotels, apartment complexes, and community facilities. While the federal law does not strictly mandate residential pool compliance, Virginia building codes adopted through the VUSBC may require compliant drain covers on new residential pool construction or major renovations. For real estate purposes, a missing, broken, or non-compliant drain cover is a red flag that should be reported to the buyer and addressed before closing. A pool inspector should verify compliance as part of any pool inspection.
VA Loans and Swimming Pools
Minimum Property Requirements — VA Pamphlet 26-7, Chapter 12

Inground Pools

  • VA appraiser must determine pool's condition and effect on property value
  • If pool is winterized or not in use, appraiser must assume it is in good working order unless evidence shows otherwise
  • Pool must not present a safety hazard
  • Pool must comply with local code (general MPR for entire property)

Above-Ground Pools

  • May be included in the appraisal if:
    • Pool includes permanent equipment (filtration, decking), AND
    • This type of installation is customary in the area
  • Without permanent equipment: considered personal property, excluded from appraisal
Key Point: VA MPRs do not have pool-specific code requirements beyond general property safety and code compliance. The appraiser's role is to assess condition and value impact, not to certify the pool. A winterized pool is assumed functional, but this does not guarantee it. Always recommend a separate pool inspection.
Safe House Property Inspections25 of 26
Speaker Notes The VA Lenders Handbook, officially known as VA Pamphlet 26-7, Chapter 12, governs the Minimum Property Requirements for VA loans. For inground pools, the appraiser must assess the pool's condition and its impact on property value. Importantly, if the pool is winterized or covered, the appraiser must assume it is in good working order unless there is visible evidence of a problem. This protects the buyer but also means that hidden defects may not be caught by the appraisal. This is why a separate pool inspection is critical for VA buyers. For above-ground pools, the key question is whether the installation is permanent (has filtration, decking) and whether such installations are customary in the area. If both are true, the pool may be appraised as part of the real estate. If not, it is personal property and excluded from the appraisal.

Answer Key (for instructor use): 1. B — 4 feet (48 inches). Code 15.2-921 defines "fence" as "not less than four feet in height above ground surface." 2. C — VGB Act. Public Law 110-140, enacted 2007. 3. B — Assume good working order. VA Pamphlet 26-7, Chapter 12. 4. B — Nothing. Pools are NOT one of the 19 covered topics under the "no representations" disclosure form. The seller makes no representations about pool condition. This is why a pool inspection is the buyer's primary protection. 5. B — Must be maintained as required by the code under which constructed. VMC 303.2.
